**Article Details for PMID: 41204807**

**Title:** Case-Based Applications of the 2025 AHA/ACC/Multispecialty High Blood Pressure Guideline.

**Authors:** Natalie A Cameron, Daniel W Jones, Sadiya S Khan, Donald M Lloyd-Jones

**Journal:** Hypertension (Dallas, Tex. : 1979)
**Publication Date:** 2025-11-19
**DOI:** 10.1161/HYPERTENSIONAHA.125.25913
**PMC ID:** 12617343
**Full Text Available:** Yes
**Full Text URL:** https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC12617343/


**Abstract:**
Hypertension affects nearly half of all adults in the United States and is the leading, preventable cause of cardiovascular disease worldwide. The American Heart Association, American College of Cardiology, and 11 other professional organizations recently published an updated 2025 guideline to reflect the latest advances in the prevention, detection, evaluation, and management of high blood pressure. To bridge the gap between this guideline update and individualized patient care, this Special Article presents 4 hypothetical cases of high blood pressure, focusing on management in the outpatient setting. These cases illustrate how to apply a risk-based approach to high blood pressure management that incorporates blood pressure levels, cardiovascular disease risk factors and the predicting risk of cardiovascular disease events cardiovascular disease equations. They also highlight notable updates in the 2025 guideline such as recommendations for lifestyle approaches, initiation of medications, blood pressure goals, primary aldosteronism screening, and management of high blood pressure before, during and after pregnancy. By contextualizing the 2025 guideline within these hypothetical case scenarios, this Special Article provides practical guidance to health care teams to offer the most up-to-date, evidence-based care of high blood pressure.

**Full Text:**
Corresponding Author: Donald M. Lloyd-Jones, MD, ScM, Boston University School of Medicine, 72 E. Concord St, L-510, Boston, MA 02118, dlloydjo@bu.edu

Hypertension affects nearly half of all adults in the United States and is the leading, preventable cause of cardiovascular disease worldwide. The American Heart Association, American College of Cardiology and 11 other professional organizations recently published an updated 2025 guideline to reflect the latest advances in the prevention, detection, evaluation and management of high blood pressure. To bridge the gap between this guideline update and individualized patient care, this Special Article presents 4 hypothetical cases of high blood pressure, focusing on management in the outpatient setting. These cases illustrate how to apply a risk-based approach to high blood pressure management that incorporates blood pressure levels, cardiovascular disease risk factors and the PREVENT-CVD equations. They also highlight notable updates in the 2025 guideline such as recommendations for lifestyle approaches, initiation of medications, blood pressure goals, primary aldosteronism screening, and management of high blood pressure before, during and after pregnancy. By contextualizing the 2025 guideline within these hypothetical case scenarios, this Special Article provides practical guidance to healthcare teams to offer the most up-to-date, evidence-based care of high blood pressure.

Keywords: antihypertensive agents, blood pressure, cardiovascular disease, hypertension, evaluation, management, risk factors

Hypertension is the leading preventable cause of cardiovascular disease (CVD) and contributes to over 10 million deaths worldwide annually.1 In the US, hypertension is defined as systolic blood pressure [BP] ≥130 mm Hg or diastolic BP ≥80 mm Hg in non-pregnant adults or receiving antihypertensive drug therapy, and it affects approximately 120 million individuals, representing nearly half of all adults.1 For women, hypertension is a major contributor during pregnancy and the postpartum period to maternal morbidity and mortality.2 Over the past decade, there have been substantial gains in the evidence base regarding the prevention and management of hypertension throughout the life course. Thus, the American Heart Association (AHA), American College of Cardiology (ACC) and 11 other professional health organizations recently published a new 2025 guideline with updated recommendations on the prevention, detection, evaluation, and management of high BP (BP) (i.e., Elevated BP, Stage 1 and Stage 2 hypertension).3,4

Effective implementation of evidence-based guidelines is key to reducing the burden of hypertension and its consequences, including CVD, chronic kidney disease, and dementia. However, translation of guideline recommendations into clinical practice presents many challenges. Successful implementation of the guideline requires not only knowledge of guideline updates, but also must account for the nuances and complexities of individual patient cases and their preferences to develop personalized patient care strategies. To help bridge the gap between guideline recommendations and clinical care, this Special Article presents four hypothetical clinical cases that discuss decision-making for BP management in the outpatient setting in the primary prevention of CVD. These cases highlight key concepts and updates from the 2025 guideline, focusing on the use of risk assessment to inform the evaluation of high BP and the decision to initiate antihypertensive medications.

A 58-year-old woman presents to your office for a preventive care visit. She has not had a preventive care visit in several years because she has “felt fine.” She scheduled this visit because her father had a myocardial infarction 3 months ago and she thought it was time for a checkup. She currently smokes half a pack of cigarettes per day. Her average BP in the office today, measured using recommended techniques,3 is 138/85 mm Hg. During a visit with her dermatologist two weeks ago, her BP was 137/86 mmHg. Her body mass index (BMI) is 26 kg/m2 and in-office electrocardiogram reveals left ventricular hypertrophy. A laboratory evaluation completed later that day reveals a total cholesterol of 170 mg/dL, high-density lipoprotein level of 40 mg/dL, estimated glomerular filtration rate of 90 mL/min/1.7m2, urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio (UACR) of 15 mg/g, and hemoglobin A1c of 5.5%. Based on these data, including UACR and HbA1c, her estimated 10-year risk for total CVD using the PREVENT-CVD equation is 9.2%.5 In addition to recommending tobacco cessation, which of the following is the next best step to manage her BP?

Recommend lifestyle modification (including tobacco cessation), then recheck her BP in 3 to 6 months and recalculate her 10-year CVD risk using the PREVENT-CVD equation

Recommend lifestyle modification and start antihypertensive medication now

Recommend lifestyle modification and start a glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonist now

Recommend lifestyle modification and start a sodium-glucose transport protein 2 inhibitor (SGLT2i) now

The correct answer is B: Recommend lifestyle modification and start antihypertensive medication now

The 2025 high BP guideline recommends that the decision to initiate antihypertensive medications should be based both on assessment of BP levels and CVD risk, in order to maximize the net benefit of drug therapy.3 In order to guide risk assessment and inform management, the guideline recommends the following routine testing among individuals with a new diagnosis of hypertension: complete blood count, serum sodium, potassium, calcium and creatinine with estimation of glomerular filtration rate, lipid profile, fasting blood glucose or A1c, thyroid-stimulating hormone, urinalysis, UACR and electrocardiogram. Antihypertensive medications should be initiated among all adults with average BP levels ≥ 140/90 mmHg (stage 2 hypertension or higher) and among those with average BPs ≥ 130/80 mmHg (stage 1 hypertension or higher) who have increased CVD risk (Class of Recommendation [COR] 1, Level of Evidence [LOE] A). This includes individuals with a history of clinical CVD (coronary heart disease, stroke and heart failure), chronic kidney disease, diabetes, or an estimated 10-year CVD risk ≥ 7.5% using the PREVENT-CVD equations (COR 1/ LOE A). This treatment strategy has been shown to be highly cost effective at 10-years compared to a more liberal treatment threshold of 140/90 for all adults without diabetes or chronic kidney disease.6 The current patient has stage 1 hypertension and a 10-year PREVENT total CVD risk estimate ≥ 7.5%. In addition, she has evidence of left ventricular hypertrophy on her electrocardiogram, indicating that she is likely at even higher risk than initially predicted.7 Antihypertensive medication should be initiated now to lower BP and reduce her risk of CVD events and total mortality in addition to lifestyle modification. Answer A (lifestyle modification only) would be insufficient management for this patient.

The American Heart Association PREVENT™ equations were developed to estimate risk of total CVD and its components of atherosclerotic CVD and heart failure.5,8 The equations were derived and validated among a diverse sample of over 6.5 million US adults aged 30 to 79 years old. The PREVENT equations newly incorporate measures of kidney function and metabolic health including estimated glomerular filtration rate and body mass index, as well as three optional predictors, UACR, hemoglobin A1c, and social deprivation index. The calculator is publicly available online at: https://professional.heart.org/en/guidelines-and-statements/prevent-risk-calculator/prevent-calculator.9

Of note, the PREVENT equations were not designed to estimate “updated risk” after lifestyle changes or addition of preventive therapy or both. This is because the “updated” risk reflects that of a different person, rather than of the current patient. For example, if this patient improves her systolic BP from 138 mmHg to 125 mmHg after the initiation of antihypertensive medication, re-entering her updated values into the PREVENT equation would result in an estimated 10-year CVD risk that would increase from 9.2% to 10.5%. This seemingly paradoxical result is because the “updated” risk reflects that of a different person who initiated antihypertensive therapy for high BP at some point in the past (and thus, on average, had more severe and longstanding exposure to BP elevations), rather than this current patient. Similarly, if this patient were to stop smoking and her systolic BP improved to 133 mmHg at her 3–6-month follow-up visit, her updated 10-year CVD risk would decrease from 9.2% to 5.7%. However, this updated score does not reflect her recent tobacco use and, therefore, likely underestimates her true CVD risk. Therefore, using the PREVENT equations to calculate an “updated risk” with new risk factor levels after lifestyle change or antihypertensive treatment will not yield accurate results, and should not be used to guide management decisions.

Several other strategies can be used to estimate updated risk. After initiating antihypertensive therapy, relative reduction of risk can be estimated using clinical trial data for intensive BP-lowering. For example, a meta-analysis of 123 BP lowering trials estimates a 20% reduction in major adverse cardiovascular events associated with each 10 mmHg reduction in systolic BP, which would decrease the patient’s absolute risk from 9.2% to 7.4%.10 In addition, the Million Hearts Longitudinal Atherosclerotic CVD Risk Assessment Tool, which is based on the 2013 Pooled Cohort Equation, was specifically developed for dynamic risk prediction with updating of risk factor levels over time.11

Answer C is not correct. The 2025 guideline recommend that GLP-1 receptor agonists may be used as an adjunct to lower BP in individuals with hypertension who have BMI ≥ 27 kg/m2 (COR 2b/ LOE B-R). This patient’s BMI is 26 kg/m2, which is below the current recommended threshold for GLP-1 receptor agonist initiation.

Answer D is not the preferred choice. Although SGLT2i may lower BP, they are recommended for patients with chronic kidney disease, diabetes or heart failure, and are not recommended for hypertension treatment alone in the absence of these comorbid conditions. BP-lowering with a first-line antihypertensive medication should be prioritized in this patient.

A 36-year-old man presents for a follow-up telehealth visit for BP management. At his annual exam six months ago, his average BP (measured twice after 5 minutes at rest with the cuff in place) was 137/82 mmHg. His 10-year PREVENT-CVD risk was estimated to be 1.3%. At that time, his healthcare team recommended lifestyle changes, weight loss, and follow-up for a repeat BP check in 3 to 6 months. Since then, he has started an exercise routine, reduced his dietary salt intake, minimized alcohol intake, and has lost 5 pounds (approximately 2% of his body weight). He recorded his BP every day for the past week using a BP cuff prescribed by his health care team and sent values via the patient portal. He checks his BP at rest and before his morning cup of coffee, places his arm at heart-level and keeps both feet on the floor during BP measurement. His home BPs are averaging in the 130s/80s mmHg. Which of the following is the next best step in managing his BP?

Recommend that he return to the office for an in-person BP check

Continue current lifestyle changes

Recommend that he additionally reduce his daily potassium intake

Continue lifestyle changes and start a single first-line antihypertensive medication

The correct answer is D: Continue lifestyle changes and start a single first-line antihypertensive medication

The 2025 guideline recommends initiation of antihypertensive therapy among adults who have stage 1 hypertension and low 10-year CVD risk (< 7.5%) if average BPs remain ≥ 130/80 mmHg after 3 to 6 months of a lifestyle intervention (COR 1/ LOE B-R), in order to prevent target organ damage and mitigate further rise in BP.3,8 This recommendation is based on data from the PREVER-Prevention trial which demonstrated lower risk of incident hypertension and lower left ventricular mass among participants with BP 120–139/80–89 mmHg who initiated antihypertensive medications after 3 months of a lifestyle intervention compared with placebo.12 First-line antihypertensive medications include thiazide-type diuretics, long-acting dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers (CCB), angiotensin converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors and angiotensin II receptor blockers (ARB) (COR 1/ LOE A). For adults with stage 1 hypertension who are close to their target BP, initiation of a single, first-line antihypertensive medication with subsequent dose titration and/or addition of another agent is a reasonable approach (COR 2a/ LOE C-EO). For those with stage 2 hypertension and for some high-risk patients with stage 1 hypertension, the guideline recommends initiation of antihypertensive medications from two different drug classes, ideally in a single-pill combination (COR 1/ LOE B-R). The average BP lowering effects associated with single and dual-antihypertensive therapies are listed in the Table 1. These data are obtained from a 2025 systemic review and meta-analysis of 484 randomized trials including over 100,000 participants with a mean baseline BP of 154/100 mmHg.13 This patient has persistent BPs in the stage 1 hypertensive range despite 6 months of lifestyle changes. Given that his BPs are close to his target (< 130/80 mmHg), initiation of a single antihypertensive agent is reasonable.

Answer A is not the preferred choice. This patient is using appropriate home BP monitoring techniques. In combination with patient education, telehealth counseling and clinical interventions, home BP monitoring is recommended to confirm suspected diagnoses of hypertension and titrate BP-lowering medications (COR 1/ LOE A). Use of health information technology with synchronous or asynchronous communication has also been shown to improve BP control and access to care (COR 1/ LOE B-R). A list of BP cuffs validated for home BP monitoring can be found at: validatebp.org/devices.14 Answer B is also not the preferred choice. Whereas this patient has successfully implemented lifestyle changes, nonetheless he continues to have stage 1 hypertension (as do almost half of US adults). This should not be viewed as a failure of lifestyle, and he should persist with his successful strategies to help continue BP control. Indeed, continued weight loss will benefit him on multiple fronts. Patient-facing materials describing recommended lifestyle changes to optimize BP control can be found at: https://www.heart.org/en/healthy-living/healthy-lifestyle/lifes-essential-8/how-to-manage-blood-pressure-fact-sheet.15 Expected BP lowering effects associated with each lifestyle change are shown in Table 2. Answer C is not correct. In the absence of chronic kidney disease, moderate potassium supplementation (not potassium reduction) is recommended to lower BP among adults with Elevated BP, Stage 1 or Stage 2 hypertension (COR 1/ LOR A).3 Potassium supplementation should ideally come from dietary sources for a total of 3,500 to 5,000 mg per day. The mean lowering in systolic BP expected from potassium supplementation among people with hypertension is approximately 6 mmHg.

A 47-year-old man with a past medical history of hypertension, obstructive sleep apnea (OSA), and obesity (BMI 35 kg/m2) presents for BP management. He has missed a few recent appointments because his bus did not arrive on time, and he cannot afford a ride-share or taxi. His average BP in the office today is 166/100 mmHg. He states that he monitors his BP at home using his watch and levels are usually in the low 140s/80s. He takes telmisartan 40 mg daily and does not miss doses. He uses his continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) machine nightly. He had a laboratory evaluation completed 6 months ago which revealed a potassium of 4.1, estimated glomerular filtration rate of 80 mL/min/1.7m2 and hemoglobin A1c of 6.0%. His 10-year PREVENT-CVD risk including his A1c is estimated to be 8.3%. In addition to recommending weight loss, which of the following is the next best step for managing his BP?

Add a thiazide-type diuretic and check plasma aldosterone and renin activity now

Add a thiazide-type diuretic, hold telmisartan for 2–4 weeks, then check plasma aldosterone and renin activity

Increase telmisartan to 80mg daily to achieve a goal BP of < 140/90 mmHg

Provide reassurance that his high BPs in the office are likely due to White Coat Effect

The correct answer is A: Add a prescription for a thiazide-type diuretic and check plasma aldosterone and renin activity now

The 2025 guideline recommends screening for primary aldosteronism in adults with hypertension and any of the following: resistant hypertension (regardless of serum potassium levels), hypokalemia (spontaneous or diuretic induced), obstructive sleep apnea, incidental adrenal mass, or family history of early-onset hypertension or stroke at < 40 years of age (COR 1/ LOE C-EO). Screening for primary aldosteronism may also be considered in all adults with stage 2 hypertension to improve rates of detection (COR 2b/ LOE C-EO).3 To minimize barriers or delays in diagnosis, the updated guideline recommends continuing most antihypertensive medication (except mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists) prior to initial screening with plasma aldosterone and renin activity levels (COR 1/ LOE C-LD). This patient has stage 2 hypertension, obstructive sleep apnea and difficulty travelling to appointments. He should be screened for primary aldosteronism now to avoid a delay in diagnosis. If screening results are negative or borderline, there is a high level of suspicion, and a confirmatory diagnosis would change management, temporarily withdrawing medications that may alter renin activity and/or aldosterone levels (e.g., beta blockers, central-alpha agonists, ACE inhibitors, ARBs, thiazide-type loop diuretics) and temporarily substituting them with noninterfering medications (e.g., nondihydropyridine CCBs, vasodilators, peripheral alpha blockers and potentially dihydropyridine CCBs) for 2–4 weeks prior to repeat testing may be considered.

Answer C is not the preferred choice. Among adults with hypertension and increased risk of CVD (10-year PREVENT-CVD Risk ≥ 7.5%), the guideline recommends a goal systolic BP < 130 mmHg with encouragement to achieve a systolic BP < 120 mmHg (COR 1/ LOE A); the recommended goal diastolic BP is < 80 mmHg (COR 1/ LOE B-R). BP goals for those with hypertension and low CVD risk are the same, but with lower levels of evidence (COR 2b/ LOE B-NR).3,8
Table S1 summarizes results from 8 randomized controlled trials that informed these recommendations for a more intensive BP lowering strategy.16–23 This patient has a 10-year CVD risk of 8.3% by PREVENT. Therefore, his goal BP should be < 130/80 mmHg or lower. In addition, this patient has uncontrolled, stage 2 hypertension. Per the guideline, an antihypertensive medication from a different drug class should be added, preferably offered in a single-pill combination with his current antihypertensive agent. Of note, this patient also has BMI of 35 kg/m2. The new guideline recommends weight loss combined with CPAP for adults living with overweight or obesity and OSA to reduce BP (COR 2a/LOE B-R).3 Initiation of a GLP1 receptor agonist may be also be considered as an adjunct to promote weight loss, lower BP and improve his OSA.3,24

Answer D is not the correct choice. In adults taking antihypertensive medications, the new guideline recommends home blood pressure monitoring to guide the titration of antihypertensive medications (COR 1/LOE A). However, the use of cuffless BP devices is not recommended in the diagnosis or management of hypertension (COR 3: No benefit/ LOE C-LD). Rather, use of validated BP cuffs should be recommended, as discussed in Case 2. In addition, the prevalence of white-coat hypertension is very low among adults with in-office BPs ≥ 160/100 mmHg. Adults with BPs in this range should be promptly treated.

A 35-year-old woman with a history of term preeclampsia without severe features 8 months ago presents to establish long-term care with a primary care clinician. Her average BP is currently 145/95 mmHg, BMI is 28 kg/m2, UACR is 0 and 10-year risk by PREVENT-CVD including UACR is estimated to be 0.5%. She is breastfeeding and would like to get pregnant again in another year. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step to manage her BP?

Provide reassurance that her preeclampsia has resolved, so she does not need additional monitoring nor treatment at this time

Start extended-release Nifedipine

Start an ACE inhibitor

Start low-dose aspirin at the start of her next pregnancy before 12 weeks of gestation

The correct answer is B: Start extended-release Nifedipine

The guideline newly incorporates recommendations regarding hypertension before, during and after pregnancy.25,26 Hypertensive disorders of pregnancy (HDP) are major risk factors for maternal and infant morbidity and mortality. HDP are classified based on their timing of onset and severity during pregnancy, and include chronic hypertension (diagnosed before pregnancy or before 20 weeks of gestation), gestational hypertension (diagnosed after 20 weeks of gestation) and preeclampsia (diagnosed after 20 weeks of gestation with evidence of proteinuria and/or additional end-organ damage). Among women with gestational hypertension or preeclampsia who have persistent BP elevations beyond approximately 12 weeks postpartum, a new diagnosis of chronic hypertension is made. Thus, this patient should be diagnosed with chronic hypertension and initiated on appropriate antihypertensive medications. For women who are pregnant or planning pregnancy, preferred antihypertensive agents are labetalol and extended-release nifedipine (COR 1/ LOE A).3 ACE inhibitors, ARBs, atenolol, direct renin inhibitors, nitroprusside and mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists should not be used in those who are planning to become pregnant or who are currently pregnant to avoid fetal harm during (COR 3: Harm/ LOE C-LD). In addition, when selecting antihypertensive medication for postpartum women, lactation status should also be taken into account. The National Institute of Child Health and Human Development Drug and Lactation Database (LactMed®) website (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501922/) provides data on concentrations of substances in breastmilk and potential impacts on the nursing infant.27 This patient has BP ≥ 140/90, is currently breastfeeding and planning a future pregnancy. Therefore, she should be started on antihypertensive treatment with either labetalol or nifedipine. Answer C is incorrect because ACE-inhibitors should be avoided in women planning pregnancy.

Of note, American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG) uses a BP threshold of ≥ 140/90 mmHg to define hypertension.28,29 Pregnant women with chronic hypertension should receive antihypertensive medications to achieve a BP < 140/90 mmHg (COR 1/ LOE B-R).3 These recommendations are based on data from the Chronic Hypertension and Pregnancy (CHAP) Trial demonstrating better pregnancy outcomes when targeting a BP < 140/90 mmHg compared with < 160/105 mmHg among women with mild, chronic hypertension.30 Data are currently lacking on ideal BP goals for women with hypertension who are planning pregnancy (i.e., < 140 / 90 mmHg vs. < 130 / 80 mmHg). Until additional data are available, it is reasonable to target a BP < 140/90 mmHg to avoid potential fetal harm. For women with gestational hypertension or preeclampsia, ACOG recommends initiating treatment at a BP threshold ≥ 160/110 mmHg.28

Answer A is not the preferred choice. Gestational hypertension and preeclampsia are associated with both short- and long-term risk of incident hypertension and CVD.31 Prevention, detection and treatment of hypertension after pregnancies complicated by these HDPs are critical to mitigating CVD risk. ACOG recommends that women with HDP have a BP check 3–10 days after delivery.28 If BPs normalize and medications are withdrawn, women should have their BP checked at least annually thereafter.3 Of note, although this patient’s preeclampsia has resolved, her history of preeclampsia should continue to be documented given that it is a risk factor for both preeclampsia in future pregnancies and CVD.3

Answer D is incorrect. The guideline recommends that individuals with hypertension who are planning to become pregnant should be counseled about using aspirin during pregnancy to prevent preeclampsia (COR 1/ LOE B -R).3 However, aspirin should be started between 12 and 28 weeks of gestation, not at the start of pregnancy.

These four cases underscore several key concepts from the new 2025 AHA/ACC/Multi-specialty guideline for high BP (Figure 1). First, each case demonstrates how to use a risk-based approach to hypertension management in primary prevention of CVD that incorporates BP levels, consideration of CVD risk factors, and the PREVENT equations.3,8 The risk-based approach to hypertension management includes the recommendation to initiate antihypertensive medications among all individuals with BP ≥ 140/90 mmHg (Case 4); those with BP ≥ 130/80 mmHg who have a history of CVD, diabetes, or chronic kidney disease, or estimated 10-year CVD risk ≥ 7.5% calculated by PREVENT-CVD (Case 1); or those with Stage 1 hypertension that persists despite 3–6 months of lifestyle modification (Case 2). For those with BPs ≥ 140/90 mmHg, initiation of antihypertensive medications from two different drug classes, ideally in a single-pill combination, is recommended (Case 3). A risk-based approach is further applied to treatment goals, with the guideline recommending a goal of < 130/80 mmHg for most adults and encouragement to achieve a systolic BP < 120 mmHg for those with elevated CVD risk (Case 3). A summary of this risk-based approach to the prevention, diagnosis and management of high BP is displayed in Figure 2.

Second, these cases highlight the updated recommendations regarding broader screening for primary aldosteronism. To improve screening rates, the guideline now recommends screening for primary aldosteronism among all individuals with resistant hypertension even in the absence of hypokalemia, as well as among those with risk factors such as obstructive sleep apnea or stage 2 hypertension (Case 3). Finally, Case 4 draws attention to new recommendations regarding the management of hypertension before, during, and after pregnancy.

Of note, these cases do not comprehensively cover all updates in the 2025 high BP guideline. Rather, these cases highlight key changes focused on the management of hypertension in the outpatient setting. Notable topics covered in the updated guideline that are not discussed in these cases include the management of severe hypertension and hypertensive emergencies, management of BP in ischemic stroke and acute intracranial hemorrhage, and appropriate use of renal denervation therapy for resistant hypertension.

Ultimately, improving BP-related outcomes will require both continued research efforts to fill evidence gaps, as well as effective implementation strategies to improve BP control and promote uptake of the updated guideline. Suggestions to improve implementation include partnering with community organizations and health systems, utilizing health information technology and employing a multidisciplinary team-based approach to hypertension care that facilitates accurate BP measurement, lifestyle change and medication uptake, adherence, and close, responsive follow up for medication titration to achieve blood pressure control quickly..3,32 These interventions must address the complex social and structural factors that drive hypertension prevention and management at the clinician, patient, health-system and public health levels to improve hypertension control and reduce the growing burden of disease.
